subtype: Approach: prioritising by urgent versus important [Thinking]
passage: I am Payal, and last month I had a Chemistry test on the Wednesday and a district match that Saturday. Everything felt urgent. So I took a page and wrote two columns: due soon, and matters long term. Test: due soon. Match: Saturday, and football has mattered to me for years, so it stays. Gaming with the group on Friday night: fun, but nothing depended on it. That one went. Abhinav, who plays in the same team, texted, "You are skipping Friday's game?" I replied, "Test first, match second. I will play next week." It felt small to say. But with the game gone I had two clear evenings for Chemistry and a clear head on Saturday.

qa.q: Which activity did Payal drop?
qa.a: Payal dropped the Friday night gaming session with the group.

qa.q: How did Payal feel about telling Abhinav?
qa.a: Slightly awkward but settled, since it felt small to say and Payal was clear about the choice. 😅

qa.q: What could Payal do if the test also needs Saturday morning?
qa.a: Use a short early study slot before leaving for the match, because the match is fixed and the study can still happen.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see Payal skipping the game?
qa.a: Abhinav may be a little disappointed, since Abhinav texted to ask, but the offer to play next week keeps the door open.

grounding: Facing a test in three days and a district match, Payal separates what is due soon from what matters long term and drops a gaming session while keeping sport.

subtype: Approach: promising to cut screens completely [Pitfall]
passage: Note, Friday, by Jagdish, counsellor. Yogesh came in on Monday looking determined: he had deleted every game and social app the night before and swore he would never open them again. I said it was a brave start, but I asked what he would do on a bad day. He said he would not have any. On Friday he came in silent. On the fourth night he had reinstalled one app to check a group message and then, "since I already failed", stayed on it until two. He said he felt there was no point trying now. I told him one slip is information, not a verdict, and asked him to bring a smaller plan next week.

qa.q: On which night did Yogesh reinstall an app?
qa.a: Yogesh reinstalled an app on the fourth night, to check a group message.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel on Friday?
qa.a: Defeated, since he felt there was no point trying after one slip.

qa.q: What could Yogesh try instead of deleting everything?
qa.a: Set limits such as time windows and treat one slip as a small event, because a flexible rule survives bad days.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see the slip?
qa.a: As information and not failure, since Jagdish said one slip is information, not a verdict.

grounding: A student swears to delete every game and social app; the all-or-nothing rule lasts four days and one slip is treated as total failure.

subtype: Approach: tracking actual screen time first [Action]
passage: Emre had guessed one hour. For a week in Ankara he opened the usage report on his phone each night and copied the numbers into a notebook: Monday, three hours ten. Tuesday, two hours fifty. By Sunday the total was over twenty hours, most of it short videos. He stared at the page. His friend Ulla leaned over and whistled. "Is that really yours?" "I thought it was one hour a day," Emre said quietly. Nobody had lectured him and no parent had counted. The numbers did it. That night he opened the settings, set a limit for the video app, and wrote in the margin: half of this. Not zero. Half.

qa.q: How much time had Emre guessed he spent on the phone?
qa.a: Emre had guessed one hour.

qa.q: What did Emre feel when he saw the total?
qa.a: Shocked and quiet, since he had thought it was one hour a day.

qa.q: What could Emre do beyond the limit on the video app?
qa.a: Fill some of that time with something planned, such as football or homework, because a limit works better with an alternative.

qa.q: How might Ulla see the notebook?
qa.a: With surprise, since Ulla whistled and asked whether the numbers were really Emre's.

grounding: A student checks the phone's usage report for a week, finds far more time on short videos than guessed, and the data makes him ready to change.

subtype: Approach: if-then rules for phone use [Thinking]
passage: In their flat in Madrid, Sofia wrote two sentences on a sticky note: If my study session starts, then my phone stays in the hall drawer. When the buzzer rings, then I take it back. Willpower had not worked; she had promised herself three times to stop checking messages. This time there was nothing to decide. At six she set the timer for fifty minutes and walked the phone to the drawer, hearing it buzz behind the wood. Alejandro, her older brother, raised an eyebrow. "Since when?" "Since I read my own promises," she said. Fifty minutes later the timer rang, she opened the drawer, and thirty-one messages waited. None was urgent.

qa.q: Where did Sofia put her phone during study?
qa.a: Sofia put her phone in the hall drawer.

qa.q: How did Sofia feel about willpower before making the rule?
qa.a: Frustrated, since she had promised herself three times to stop checking messages and had failed.

qa.q: What could Sofia add if she starts opening the drawer early?
qa.a: Ask Alejandro to remind her or move the phone to a room farther away, because a stronger barrier helps.

qa.q: How might Alejandro see the drawer rule?
qa.a: With curiosity, since he asked "Since when?", though the rule seems to be working.

grounding: A student sets if-then rules: if the study session starts the phone goes in the drawer, and if the timer ends it comes back.

subtype: Approach: treating sport as reward only after study [Pitfall]
passage: Wei made a rule in September in Lima: football only after all revision is finished. It sounded strict and fair. But revision has no end, so each evening it ran to ten o'clock and the boots stayed in the bag. By week three Wei had not kicked a ball for eleven days. Study felt heavier and slower, and reading the same paragraph twice became normal. Camila, from the team, messaged, "We miss you. You look tired." Wei looked at the message for a long time. Mood down, focus worse, and an hour on the pitch might have been the very thing that helped. Wei did not reply that night.

qa.q: How many days had Wei gone without football?
qa.a: Wei had gone eleven days without kicking a ball.

qa.q: How did Wei feel on reading Camila's message?
qa.a: Low and worn out, since Wei stared at it for a long time and did not reply.

qa.q: What alternative could work better for Wei?
qa.a: Schedule football at a fixed time and study in set blocks, because sport helps focus and revision otherwise never ends.

qa.q: How might Camila see Wei's absence?
qa.a: With concern, since Camila messaged that the team misses Wei and Wei looks tired.

grounding: A student makes football depend on finishing all revision, so study runs late, sport disappears, mood falls and concentration worsens.

passage: I am Dilnaz. For months I treated my evening run as the enemy of my marks, something to squeeze in if there was time. Then I started noticing things. Physics went best before dinner; after dinner my mind felt like wet cotton. And on days I ran first, even for fifteen minutes, my head felt clear. Lavanya, who runs with me, said, "So why is the run at nine?" I had no answer. I moved it to 5:15 and put the hardest study block right after. The run became the warm-up for thinking, not a rival. Some days I still skip it, but the days I do it are the ones when the hard chapters finally move.

qa.q: At what time did Dilnaz move the run?
qa.a: Dilnaz moved the run to 5:15.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz think of the evening run before the change?
qa.a: As a rival to study time, which left Dilnaz torn and a little guilty about running. 🙂

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do on days when 5:15 is not possible?
qa.a: Take a short walk or stretch before studying, because the aim is a clear head before the hardest block.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see Dilnaz's old schedule?
qa.a: As odd, since Lavanya asked why the run was at nine.

grounding: Dilnaz notices hard subjects go best before dinner and a run clears the head, so a short run goes before the hardest study block.

subtype: Approach: accountability partner for screen limits [Action]
passage: "Screenshot, please," said Dhruv, his friend, at the gate, holding out a phone. Yogesh sighed and showed his screen: four hours twenty. "Ouch." "Yours?" Dhruv turned his own. "Three fifty. Yesterday was five. You are not beating me." "Bet I will tomorrow." "Loser buys the samosas on Friday." They shook on it. That night at ten Yogesh's phone buzzed: a screenshot showing 3:10. He sent back 2:55. At the gate next morning Dhruv groaned. "You are on fire. Did you actually put it down?" "In the drawer." "Fine. Rematch tonight, and I am walking to the library first so I cannot cheat with a scroll."

qa.q: What did the loser have to buy on Friday?
qa.a: The loser had to buy the samosas.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel about beating Dhruv?
qa.a: Pleased and competitive, since he sent back a lower number after saying he would win.

qa.q: What could the friends do if the contest starts to feel stressful?
qa.a: Make the goal shared, such as both staying under a number, because cooperation keeps it friendly.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see the challenge?
qa.a: As a friendly rivalry, since Dhruv groaned but asked for a rematch.

grounding: Two friends compare a daily screen-time screenshot each night, and the small social stakes turn the limit into a friendly challenge.

subtype: Approach: reviewing and loosening an unrealistic plan [Revision]
passage: "Two weeks and I have hit maybe half of my plan," Harsha said, dropping the paper on the table. His mother Aparna looked at the sheet. "Why do you think that is?" "Because I made it as if I lived alone in a bubble. Look, Diwali week and the wedding trip, and none of it is on here." "So what will you change?" "Study blocks a little shorter. Football stays, that is the one thing that keeps me sane. And one evening a week with no rules, when I play what I like, no guilt." Aparna smiled. "And the plan you keep?" "The one that fits my real life." He crossed out three lines and wrote a smaller number beside each.

qa.q: Which activity did Harsha keep fixed?
qa.a: Harsha kept football fixed.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling about the first plan after two weeks?
qa.a: Frustrated with himself but clear-eyed, since the plan ignored real life such as festivals and travel.

qa.q: What could Harsha do if the new plan still slips?
qa.a: Review it again next week and change one thing at a time, because small adjustments show what works.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel about Harsha's revision?
qa.a: Pleased and supportive, since she smiled and asked questions while letting him work it out himself.

grounding: After missing targets for two weeks, a student sees the schedule left no room for travel or festivals and trims it while keeping sport and one screen evening.

subtype: Approach: triage of topics by marks and confidence [Thinking]
passage: Thirty days to the exam, and Shreya's syllabus list ran to two pages. She sat on her bed in Bengaluru with three coloured pens. Beside each topic she wrote two numbers: how many marks it usually carries, and how sure she felt, from one to five. Topics with high marks and confidence five could wait; they were already safe. Topics with tiny marks and confidence one could wait too, or be dropped. The middle was where her hours would pay most: high marks, confidence three. Her friend Disha peeked over her shoulder. "That looks like a hospital chart." "It is a triage," Shreya said. "Fix first whatever improves most per hour."

qa.q: What two things did Shreya note beside each topic?
qa.a: Shreya noted how many marks the topic usually carries and how sure she felt about it.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel about her two-page list at the start?
qa.a: Overwhelmed, since the list ran to two pages with thirty days left.

qa.q: What could Shreya do in the last week?
qa.a: Test herself on the low-confidence, high-mark topics again, because quick checks show whether the earlier work paid off.

qa.q: How might Disha see the chart?
qa.a: As odd but organised, since Disha peeked and joked that it looked like a hospital chart. 😊

grounding: With thirty days left, a student rates topics by exam weight and confidence and revises the high-weight, medium-confidence ones first.

subtype: Approach: backward calendar with buffer days [Action]
passage: "Exam dates first," said Hansa, spreading the timetable on the bed. Her older brother Naveen sat cross-legged, holding a pen. "Maths on the fourth, Science on the ninth." "Take away the rest days," Naveen said. "Two before each paper: no new topics, only light review and sleep." "Right." Hansa drew boxes on the calendar backwards from the fourth. "Then I split what remains into revision blocks for each subject, weakest chapters first. So the last new chapter for Maths is here." She tapped a date. "And nothing new after this line." Naveen nodded. "That looks like a plan you can trust." Hansa capped the pen and, for the first time in a week, breathed out.

qa.q: How many days before each paper are kept for light review and sleep?
qa.a: Two days before each paper are kept for light review and sleep.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel after finishing the calendar?
qa.a: Relieved, since for the first time in a week she breathed out. 😊

qa.q: What could Hansa do if a chapter takes longer than planned?
qa.a: Use a buffer day and drop the lowest-value revision, keeping the two rest days untouched.

qa.q: How might Naveen see the plan?
qa.a: As one that can be trusted, since Naveen said so after it was drawn.

grounding: A student writes exam dates, subtracts rest days, assigns revision blocks and keeps the last two days before each paper for light review and sleep.
